value.overview: The Red-breasted Meadowlark (Leistes militaris) is a medium-sized grassland bird of the New World tropics. Adult males are strikingly black above and below with a vivid red throat, breast, and shoulder patch. Females and juveniles are browner, less strongly marked, and show only limited reddish coloration. It belongs to the blackbird family, Icteridae, and is often found in open, wet country rather than forest interiors.
value.classification: The Red-breasted Meadowlark is a passerine in the family Icteridae. It is the only species currently placed in the genus Leistes militaris, although it was formerly treated under Sturnella.
value.identification: Adults are about 18–19 cm long. The male has a black head, back, wings, and underparts, contrasting sharply with a red throat, breast, and shoulder area; the red can appear especially bright during display. The female is duller, with brown upperparts, pale or buff underparts, and weaker reddish tones. Juveniles resemble females but are generally paler. In Costa Rica, it may be distinguished from other meadowlarks by its extensive black plumage and red breast rather than a pale eyebrow or strongly streaked appearance.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southwestern Costa Rica through Panama and northern South America, including Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Trinidad, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident breeder, concentrated in the Golfo Dulce region and extending north at least to the Sierpe–Palmar area. It uses open, humid habitats such as wet grasslands, cattle pasture, savannas, rice fields, lightly wooded clearings, and grassy areas with scattered shrubs, posts, or small trees.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident or partly migratory. In Costa Rica, birds may disappear from breeding areas during the nonbreeding season, but it is uncertain whether this reflects true migration or local movements; the species is not treated as a regular long-distance migrant there.
value.breeding: Breeding information from Costa Rica is limited, but nesting has been reported mainly around May. The species builds a deep, open cup of grass on or very near the ground, usually concealed within tall or overhanging vegetation. Clutches generally contain two to four cream-colored eggs marked with reddish-brown blotches. Males sing from low perches and perform a display flight, rising several metres before descending with partly closed wings while singing. Nesting may occur in loose colonies or clustered pairs.
value.dietFeeding: The Red-breasted Meadowlark forages mainly on the ground in short or moderately tall grass. Its diet consists chiefly of insects and other small invertebrates, supplemented by seeds and occasionally berries or cultivated grains such as rice. It walks and probes through vegetation and bare ground, taking prey and plant food from the surface or among grass stems. Feeding groups may form outside the breeding season when food is abundant.
value.behavior: Males defend breeding areas with song, prominent perches, and aerial display flights. Their song is delivered from fence posts, bushes, or other low elevated sites, and the male may rise and parachute downward while singing. Outside the breeding period, individuals can gather in loose flocks and may roost communally. The species is active by day, alert, and strongly associated with open ground where it can walk, forage, and rapidly take flight when disturbed.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species has a broad range and is not currently considered globally threatened. In Costa Rica, its distribution is localized and may vary between years.
